summary:
Gabon has no law criminalising same-sex intimacy. The same conduct was nonetheless prohibited between July 2019 and July 2020, and that episode is the best guide to how quickly the position can move. Gabon gained independence in 1960 with no inherited colonial-era sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was not an offence until the new penal code, Law 042/2018, entered into force on 5 July 2019.

The 2019 code did not name homosexuality. Article 402 listed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" within "atteintes aux mœurs", exposing those convicted to up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, roughly US$8,500. Enforcement was not theoretical: two men were arrested within months of enactment and released only after paying police bribes, a pattern the US Department of State documented in its 2019 country report alongside societal discrimination.

The National Assembly overturned the ban in July 2020, restoring the pre-2019 position in which same-sex relations between men and women were lawful nationwide. The reversal divided public opinion sharply, and Gabon's current decriminalised status rests on ordinary legislation rather than an entrenched constitutional settlement.

That settlement arrived at referendum on 16 November 2024, when the constitution adopted by the military government that took power in the August 2023 coup ending 56 years of Bongo-family rule was approved by more than 90% of voters on turnout of about 55%. Civil society had demanded the re-criminalisation of homosexuality during the drafting; that demand lost. The adopted text instead protects privacy under Article 18 in terms read as protective of LGBTI people. Article 16, however, defines marriage in a way that excludes same-sex couples, so the constitution blocks criminalisation while also blocking marriage equality.

There is no legal gender recognition in Gabon, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. A visitor presenting documents in a gender inconsistent with the marker on their passport should expect no domestic legal remedy for discrepancies, and there is no registered community machinery that would receive or advise a trans traveller. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records both absences, as well as the same-sex relations position as legal nationwide since the 2020 repeal.

Nothing in the sources documents arrests, prosecutions or detentions of LGBTI people since the 2020 repeal, but the 2019–2020 period shows what can happen within weeks of a change in the law, including arrests settled by police bribes rather than charges. Conservative social attitudes remain widely held, and discrimination is documented rather than hypothetical. Discretion in public life remains prudent, and the constitutional privacy protection is a legal guarantee, not a guarantee of social tolerance.
tangentialFactors:
The 2019–2020 reversal is the jurisdiction's defining fact for comparison with neighbouring countries: Gabon criminalised same-sex conduct for a single year, in a region where many states retain colonial-era prohibitions, and repealed it before an international human rights reporting cycle could establish an enforcement record. Gabon's independence in 1960 came without a sodomy statute, so the 2019 code imported rather than inherited the offence.

The November 2024 referendum places LGBTI legal status inside a wider constitutional overhaul driven by a military government that ended a 56-year family dynasty. High turnout and an overwhelming yes vote indicate broad acceptance of the document as a whole, not necessarily broad support for its Article 18 privacy protections, which is why the re-criminalisation demand that failed during drafting cannot be treated as a measure of public opinion.

Article 16 is the clearest instance in the sources of a jurisdiction where decriminalisation and the exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage coexist within a single constitutional text. The registration ban on LGBTI groups removes the institutional base that would otherwise press for the partner-recognition and gender-recognition law that does not exist.
localsOnly:
Residents of Gabon face no criminal penalty for same-sex relations. The repeal by the National Assembly in July 2020 restored the position that prevailed from independence until July 2019, when Law 042/2018 took effect and Article 402 filed same-sex relations under offences against public morals, carrying up to six months in prison and a five million CFA franc fine.

Same-sex marriage is unavailable. Article 16 of the constitution adopted at the 16 November 2024 referendum defines marriage in terms that exclude same-sex couples, and Article 18's privacy guarantee does not alter that definition.

No procedure for legal gender recognition exists, and no domestic legal mechanism is available for correcting the gender marker on identity documents.

LGBTI organisations cannot register. Community advocacy, support networks and any formally constituted protection machinery operate without legal standing, which leaves residents without institutional recourse in cases of discrimination or police mistreatment.

Discrimination against LGBTI people is documented in official reporting, including the US Department of State's 2019 human rights report, and the period of criminalisation saw arrests settled by police bribes. Social conservatism and the absence of anti-discrimination legislation shape daily life regardless of the repeal.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents whether Article 18 of the 2024 constitution has been invoked in any court proceeding, and no case law on privacy-based LGBTI claims is available. Its practical effect on enforcement is therefore unresolved.

Nothing here addresses hate-crime sentencing, police training, or any official protection mechanism for LGBTI people beyond the constitutional privacy text; the inventory contains no data on such provisions, and their absence should not be inferred as proof that none exists.

Access to gender-affirming care, HIV services and other trans-specific health provision is not covered by any source provided, so the map carries no assessment of it.

No post-2020 arrest, detention or prosecution data appears in the inventory. The 2019 arrests are the only enforcement incidents sourced here, and they are reported by a single outlet whose account of the two men's release through police bribes is not independently corroborated in the inventory.

Visa, entry and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers is not sourced for Gabon. The fine figures for the 2019 offence vary slightly between sources, given as 5,000,000 CFA francs, about US$8,500 and about US$8,561, reflecting exchange-rate timing rather than a difference in the statute.
